title: QLoRA: Fine-tuning Quantized LLMs
hook: Fine-tune a model with tens of billions of parameters on a single GPU. QLoRA squeezes the frozen base to 4-bit, then trains LoRA adapters on top — without losing quality.
key_points: Quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit to cut memory, then trains LoRA adapters on top.
Brings fine-tuning of very large models within reach of a single GPU.
Introduces a 4-bit NormalFloat data type, double quantization, and paged optimizers to save memory.
Matches the quality of 16-bit fine-tuning despite the aggressive quantization.
content_html: Tim Dettmers and colleagues combined two ideas to make fine-tuning huge models cheap. QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit precision to slash memory, then trains LoRA adapters on top of it. The trick is that the heavy frozen weights barely cost anything, while the small adapters do the learning — and the result holds up against full 16-bit fine-tuning.
extra_html:
How it works

QLoRA keeps the base model frozen and quantized to 4-bit, so it occupies a fraction of the usual memory. During training, those 4-bit weights are dequantized on the fly to compute activations, but no gradients flow into them — only the LoRA adapters get updated. The paper adds three tricks to make this work cleanly: a 4-bit NormalFloat type tuned for normally-distributed weights, double quantization that even compresses the quantization constants, and paged optimizers that offload memory spikes to avoid running out during training.

Why it matters

Before QLoRA, customizing the largest open models often meant renting a cluster. By driving the memory footprint down far enough, it let researchers and hobbyists fine-tune models that previously needed many GPUs on a single one — all while preserving quality. That accessibility helped spark a wave of community fine-tunes of open-weight models.

related.hook: Why retrain billions of weights when you can freeze them all and train tiny add-on matrices instead? LoRA tunes under ~1% of the parameters with near-full-fine-tune quality.

related.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Inference for Transformers
related.hook: Big transformers usually run in 16-bit. LLM.int8() halves that to 8-bit integers without losing accuracy — by treating a few rare 'outlier' features with care.
